claim: Over 170 different mutations in the gene encoding SOD1 all cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Over 170 different mutations in the gene encoding SOD1 all cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge in the field and is stated in the abstract.

claim: Misfolding of ALS-linked SOD1 mutants and wild-type (wt) SOD1 exposes a normally buried nuclear export signal (NES)-like sequence.
source: Here, we show that misfolding of ALS-linked SOD1 mutants and wild-type (wt) SOD1 exposes a normally buried nuclear export signal (NES)-like sequence.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including structural analysis and antibody recognition experiments.

claim: The nuclear export carrier protein CRM1 recognizes the NES-like sequence and exports misfolded SOD1 to the cytoplasm.
source: The nuclear export carrier protein CRM1 recognizes this NES-like sequence and exports misfolded SOD1 to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including CRM1 inhibition experiments, knockdown studies, and pull-down assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: Antibodies against the NES-like sequence recognize misfolded SOD1, but not native wt SOD1 both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Antibodies against the NES-like sequence recognize misfolded SOD1, but not native wt SOD1 both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation, immunofluorescence, and immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disruption of the NES consensus sequence relocalizes mutant SOD1 to the nucleus, resulting in higher toxicity in cells.
source: Disruption of the NES consensus sequence relocalizes mutant SOD1 to the nucleus, resulting in higher toxicity in cells, and severer impairments in locomotion, egg-laying, and survival in Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assays and C. elegans phenotypic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disruption of the NES consensus sequence causes severer impairments in locomotion, egg-laying, and survival in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Disruption of the NES consensus sequence relocalizes mutant SOD1 to the nucleus, resulting in higher toxicity in cells, and severer impairments in locomotion, egg-laying, and survival in Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: This is supported by C. elegans behavioral and survival assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: SOD1 mutants are removed from the nucleus by CRM1 as a defense mechanism against proteotoxicity of misfolded SOD1 in the nucleus.
source: Our data suggest that SOD1 mutants are removed from the nucleus by CRM1 as a defense mechanism against proteotoxicity of misfolded SOD1 in the nucleus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including toxicity assays and phenotypic analyses.

claim: About 10% of ALS cases have positive family history and are classified as familial ALS (fALS).
source: About 10% of ALS cases have positive family history and are classified as familial ALS (fALS).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field cited in the introduction.

claim: 90% of ALS cases are classified as sporadic ALS (sALS).
source: The remaining 90% of ALS cases are classified as sporadic ALS (sALS).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field cited in the introduction.

claim: Mutations in over 40 genes have been associated with fALS.
source: Mutations in over 40 genes have been associated with fALS (Ajroud-Driss and Siddique, 2015), including the first identified gene encoding Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (SOD1) (Deng et al., 1993; Rosen et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SOD1 was the first identified gene associated with fALS.
source: Mutations in over 40 genes have been associated with fALS (Ajroud-Driss and Siddique, 2015), including the first identified gene encoding Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (SOD1) (Deng et al., 1993; Rosen et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original discovery papers.

claim: Over 170 mutations involving 88 of the 154 amino acids of SOD1 have been identified in patients diagnosed with ALS.
source: To date, over 170 mutations involving 88 of the 154 amino acids of SOD1 have been identified in patients diagnosed with ALS (Taylor et al., 2016) (alsod.iop.kcl.uk).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a database and previous literature.

claim: Mutations in SOD1 account for about 20% of familial ALS cases.
source: Mutations in SOD1 account for about 20% of familial and 2–7% of sporadic ALS cases (alsod.iop.kcl.uk), which makes SOD1 the second most frequently mutated gene after C9ORF72 in affected Caucasians (Ajroud-Driss and Siddique, 2015; Renton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a database and previous literature.

claim: Mutations in SOD1 account for 2–7% of sporadic ALS cases.
source: Mutations in SOD1 account for about 20% of familial and 2–7% of sporadic ALS cases (alsod.iop.kcl.uk), which makes SOD1 the second most frequently mutated gene after C9ORF72 in affected Caucasians (Ajroud-Driss and Siddique, 2015; Renton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a database and previous literature.

claim: SOD1 is the second most frequently mutated gene after C9ORF72 in affected Caucasians.
source: Mutations in SOD1 account for about 20% of familial and 2–7% of sporadic ALS cases (alsod.iop.kcl.uk), which makes SOD1 the second most frequently mutated gene after C9ORF72 in affected Caucasians (Ajroud-Driss and Siddique, 2015; Renton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SOD1 is a highly conserved and ubiquitously expressed free-radical scavenging enzyme.
source: SOD1 is a highly conserved and ubiquitously expressed free-radical scavenging enzyme.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SOD1 function.

claim: SOD1 catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide radical (O2.−) into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
source: It catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide radical (O2.−) into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), which in turn is reduced to water and oxygen by catalase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SOD1 enzymatic function.

claim: SOD1 comprises 1–2% of the total soluble protein in the nervous system.
source: SOD1 is highly abundant, comprising 1–2% of the total soluble protein in the nervous system (Pardo et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SOD1 knockout mice failed to develop an ALS-like phenotype.
source: Despite its important physiological function, SOD1 knockout mice failed to develop an ALS-like phenotype (Reaume et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A toxic gain-of-function in SOD1 mutants is a fundamental mechanism for the pathogenesis of ALS.
source: Increasing evidence indicates that a toxic gain-of-function in SOD1 mutants is a fundamental mechanism for the pathogenesis of ALS (Williamson et al., 2000; Deng et al., 2006; Sau et al., 2007; Rotunno and Bosco, 2013; Bunton-Stasyshyn et al., 2015; Silverman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to multiple previous studies.

claim: Many toxic effects caused by SOD1 mutants have been reported, including excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, axonal transport disruption, prion-like propagation, and non-cell autonomous toxicity of neuroglia.
source: Although the exact mechanisms by which diverse SOD1 mutations all cause ALS remains unclear, many toxic effects caused by SOD1 mutants have been reported, including excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, axonal transport disruption, prion-like propagation, and non-cell autonomous toxicity of neuroglia (Hayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Aggregation of SOD1 mutants in motor neurons is a common pathological feature.
source: Aggregation of SOD1 mutants in motor neurons is a common pathological feature.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Removal of SOD1 mutants through degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system and autophagy reduces their cytotoxicity.
source: Indeed, it has been reported that removal of SOD1 mutants through degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system and autophagy, or through induction of heat shock proteins reduces their cytotoxicity (Kabuta et al., 2006; Tan et al., 2008; Ying et al., 2009; Crippa et al., 2010; Kalmar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Induction of heat shock proteins reduces SOD1 mutant cytotoxicity.
source: Indeed, it has been reported that removal of SOD1 mutants through degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system and autophagy, or through induction of heat shock proteins reduces their cytotoxicity (Kabuta et al., 2006; Tan et al., 2008; Ying et al., 2009; Crippa et al., 2010; Kalmar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SOD1 is normally localized in both the cytoplasm and the nucleus of cells.
source: SOD1 is normally localized in both the cytoplasm and the nucleus of cells (Crapo et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: GFP-SOD1wt is evenly distributed in the cytoplasm and the nucleus when expressed in HeLa cells.
source: We found that when GFP-tagged wt-SOD1 (GFP-SOD1wt) and two mutants (GFP-SOD1G85R and GFP-SOD1G93A) were expressed in HeLa cells, both mutants showed predominantly cytoplasmic distribution while GFP-SOD1wt was evenly distributed in the cytoplasm and the nucleus as expected (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GFP-SOD1G85R and GFP-SOD1G93A show predominantly cytoplasmic distribution when expressed in HeLa cells.
source: We found that when GFP-tagged wt-SOD1 (GFP-SOD1wt) and two mutants (GFP-SOD1G85R and GFP-SOD1G93A) were expressed in HeLa cells, both mutants showed predominantly cytoplasmic distribution while GFP-SOD1wt was evenly distributed in the cytoplasm and the nucleus as expected (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Leptomycin B (LMB) treatment causes SOD1G85R and SOD1G93A mutants to accumulate in the nucleus.
source: Impairment of the CRM1-dependent nuclear export pathway with a CRM1 inhibitor, leptomycin B (LMB), caused the mutants to accumulate in the nucleus (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Knockdown of CRM1 expression by RNAi leads to accumulation of SOD1 mutants in the nucleus.
source: Similarly, knockdown of CRM1 expression by RNAi or co-expression of a Q69L mutant of Ran GTPase, a dominant-negative inhibitor of CRM1 (Xu et al., 2010; Kehlenbach et al., 1999), also led to accumulation of the mutants in the nucleus (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Co-expression of RanQ69L mutant leads to accumulation of SOD1 mutants in the nucleus.
source: Similarly, knockdown of CRM1 expression by RNAi or co-expression of a Q69L mutant of Ran GTPase, a dominant-negative inhibitor of CRM1 (Xu et al., 2010; Kehlenbach et al., 1999), also led to accumulation of the mutants in the nucleus (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: RanQ69L is a dominant-negative inhibitor of CRM1.
source: Similarly, knockdown of CRM1 expression by RNAi or co-expression of a Q69L mutant of Ran GTPase, a dominant-negative inhibitor of CRM1 (Xu et al., 2010; Kehlenbach et al., 1999), also led to accumulation of the mutants in the nucleus (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Proteasome inhibition for 60 min did not significantly affect the nuclear levels of GFP-SOD1G85R.
source: Proteasome inhibition for 60 min did not significantly affect the nuclear levels of GFP-SOD1G85R but again LMB treatment did (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LMB treatment significantly affects the nuclear levels of GFP-SOD1G85R.
source: Proteasome inhibition for 60 min did not significantly affect the nuclear levels of GFP-SOD1G85R but again LMB treatment did (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The lack of nuclear distribution of SOD1 mutants is mediated by CRM1-dependent nuclear export.
source: These results suggest that the lack of nuclear distribution of SOD1 mutants is mediated by CRM1-dependent nuclear export.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: CRM1 exports its physiological cargo proteins through the recognition of the leucine-rich nuclear export signal (NES).
source: It is well known that CRM1 exports its physiological cargo proteins through the recognition of the leucine-rich nuclear export signal (NES) (Kosugi et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Selective export of mutant but not wt SOD1 suggests that SOD1 does not have a physiological NES.
source: Selective export of mutant but not wt SOD1 suggests that SOD1 does not have a physiological NES.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that only mutant SOD1 is exported.

claim: Fusion of peptide P1 (residues 24–55 of SOD1) with mCherry results in nuclear clearance of mCherry.
source: The peptides were each fused to mCherry and expressed in HeLa cells. Fusion with peptide P1 corresponding to residues 24–55 of SOD1, but not with P2 resulted in the nuclear clearance of mCherry, which could be restored by LMB treatment (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Fusion of peptide P2 with mCherry does not result in nuclear clearance of mCherry.
source: The peptides were each fused to mCherry and expressed in HeLa cells. Fusion with peptide P1 corresponding to residues 24–55 of SOD1, but not with P2 resulted in the nuclear clearance of mCherry, which could be restored by LMB treatment (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: P1 peptide interacts with CRM1 protein in GST pull-down experiments.
source: GST pull-down experiments showed that P1 and the NES from protein kinase inhibitor (PKI) (Güttler et al., 2010) as a positive control, but not P2, interact with CRM1 protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: P2 peptide does not interact with CRM1 protein in GST pull-down experiments.
source: GST pull-down experiments showed that P1 and the NES from protein kinase inhibitor (PKI) (Güttler et al., 2010) as a positive control, but not P2, interact with CRM1 protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Peptide P1 in human SOD1 contains a functional NES consensus sequence.
source: These results suggest that peptide P1 in human SOD1 contains a functional NES consensus sequence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Five hydrophobic residues (I35, L38, L42, F45, and V47) in P1 are essential for G93A nuclear export.
source: Eight hydrophobic residues in P1 are among the candidates for the NES consensus residues, and therefore, each was mutated to Arginine (R) in GFP-SOD1G93A. Five of the resulting mutants, including I35R, L38R, L42R, F45R, and V47R, showed even distribution in the cytoplasm and the nucleus, suggesting these five hydrophobic residues are essential for G93A nuclear export (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The essential residues for nuclear export are in good agreement with the PKI-class NES consensus.
source: These essential residues are in good agreement with the PKI-class NES consensus Φ0-X2-Φ1-X3-Φ2-X2–3-Φ3-X-Φ4 (Güttler et al., 2010) (Figure 2E), where Φ0-Φ4 are five key hydrophobic residues spaced by different number of amino acids (denoted as Xn) that are preferentially charged, polar or small.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2E and citation to previous literature.

claim: Leu42 is not conserved in orthologs for human SOD1.
source: Importantly, sequence alignment revealed that one of the five essential hydrophobic residues, Leu42 (Φ2), is not conserved in orthologs for human SOD1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mutation of Leu42 to Glutamine (as in mouse SOD1) abolishes the nuclear export ability of GFP-SOD1G93A.
source: Mutation of this residue to Glutamine (Q), as is naturally present in the mouse ortholog, abolished the nuclear export ability of GFP-SOD1G93A (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: P1 is not an evolutionarily conserved physiological NES.
source: These results indicate that P1 is not an evolutionarily conserved physiological NES but may be exposed by misfolding of SOD1 mutants.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of conservation of key residues across species.

claim: P1 may be exposed by misfolding of SOD1 mutants.
source: These results indicate that P1 is not an evolutionarily conserved physiological NES but may be exposed by misfolding of SOD1 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing selective export of mutant SOD1.

claim: The NES-like consensus sequence (aa35-47) forms part of strand β3, the crossover loop, and strand β4 in wt-SOD1 structure.
source: The NES-like consensus sequence (aa35-47) forms part of strand β3, the crossover loop, and strand β4, and is almost completely buried in the structure (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The NES-like consensus sequence is almost completely buried in the wt-SOD1 structure.
source: The NES-like consensus sequence (aa35-47) forms part of strand β3, the crossover loop, and strand β4, and is almost completely buried in the structure (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Leu42 is the only one of the five essential hydrophobic residues exposed on the protein surface in wt-SOD1.
source: In fact, Leu42 is the only one of the five essential hydrophobic residues exposed on the protein surface (Figure 3A), which may explain why natural substitution of Leu42 by Gln in mouse SOD1 does not affect its structure (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Natural substitution of Leu42 by Gln in mouse SOD1 does not affect its structure.
source: In fact, Leu42 is the only one of the five essential hydrophobic residues exposed on the protein surface (Figure 3A), which may explain why natural substitution of Leu42 by Gln in mouse SOD1 does not affect its structure (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation and sequence alignment.

claim: CRM1 is precipitated by all four ALS-linked mutants tested (Q22L, G85R, G93A, and L144S) but not by wt-SOD1 in GST pull-down assays.
source: CRM1 was precipitated by all four ALS-linked mutants tested, including Q22L, G85R, G93A, and L144S, but not by wt-SOD1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: L38R mutation in G85R or G93A largely diminishes their binding to CRM1.
source: Disruption of the NES consensus sequence by creating an L38R mutation in G85R or G93A largely diminished their binding to CRM1 (Figure 3B, Lane 7 vs 4, Lane 8 vs 5).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CRM1-NES-like sequence interaction is dependent on the presence of RanGTP.
source: Moreover, CRM1-NES-like sequence interaction was dependent on the presence of RanGTP. The interaction was diminished when RanGTP was omitted from the pull-down assay (Figure 3C), indicating a receptor-cargo relationship for CRM1-NES-like sequence of SOD1.
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The CRM1-NES-like sequence interaction indicates a receptor-cargo relationship.
source: Moreover, CRM1-NES-like sequence interaction was dependent on the presence of RanGTP. The interaction was diminished when RanGTP was omitted from the pull-down assay (Figure 3C), indicating a receptor-cargo relationship for CRM1-NES-like sequence of SOD1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RanGTP-dependent interaction data.

claim: Anti-NLP efficiently precipitates GFP-SOD1G93A and six other mutants but not GFP-SOD1wt under native conditions.
source: Under native condition, anti-NLP efficiently precipitated GFP-SOD1G93A and six other mutants but not GFP-SOD1wt from lysates prepared from HEK293T cells transiently expressing the respective protein (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by native immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: The NES-like sequence of SOD1 is normally buried in the wild-type protein but is exposed in the mutants possibly due to protein misfolding.
source: These results indicate that the NES-like sequence of SOD1 is normally buried in the wild-type protein but is exposed in the mutants possibly due to protein misfolding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural and biochemical data presented.

claim: Exposure of the NES-like sequence is a common feature for all 17 representative ALS-linked SOD1 mutants tested.
source: The GST pull-down and IP results also suggest that the NES-like sequence is exposed in multiple ALS-linked SOD1 mutants. We then asked whether exposure of the NES-like sequence is a common feature for ALS-linked SOD1 mutants. We tested 17 representative ALS-linked SOD1 mutants, including those deficient in copper binding (H46R, H48R, and H120L) or zinc binding (H80R and D83G) and one that cannot form disulfide bond (C57R) (Valentine et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by data from multiple experiments testing 17 different mutants.

claim: Positive anti-NLP staining was found in 90–100% of cells for all mutants except for L126S (81%) and L144S (77%).
source: Positive anti-NLP staining was found in 90–100% of cells for all mutants except for L126S (81%) and L144S (77%) (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A, 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: All SOD1 mutants tested expose the NES-like sequence, but the propensities to expose it vary among the mutants.
source: These results suggest that all SOD1 mutants tested expose the NES-like sequence, but the propensities to expose it vary among the mutants.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunofluorescence and immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Mutants with less N<C GFP distribution (H46R, D90A, L126S and L144S) were less efficiently precipitated by anti-NLP compared to mutants showing predominant N<C GFP distribution (A4V, G85R, G93A and G108V).
source: Native IP with anti-NLP antibodies further confirmed that mutants with less N<C GFP distribution (H46R, D90A, L126S and L144S) were also less efficiently precipitated by anti-NLP, compared to mutants showing predominant N<C GFP distribution (A4V, G85R, G93A and G108V) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by native immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ALS patients with H46R, D90A, L126S or L144S mutation have slow disease progression.
source: Interestingly, available reports indicate that ALS patients with H46R, D90A, L126S or L144S mutation have slow disease progression, whereas disease progress faster in patients with A4V, G85R, G93A or G108V mutation (Bali et al., 2017; Byström et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Disease progresses faster in ALS patients with A4V, G85R, G93A or G108V mutation.
source: Interestingly, available reports indicate that ALS patients with H46R, D90A, L126S or L144S mutation have slow disease progression, whereas disease progress faster in patients with A4V, G85R, G93A or G108V mutation (Bali et al., 2017; Byström et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SOD1 mutants' tendencies to expose the NES-like sequence correlate with disease progression.
source: It is possible that SOD1 mutants can assume more than one conformations in cells, among which their tendencies to expose the NES-like sequence correlate with disease progression.
evidence: This is speculation based on the correlation observed between NES exposure and disease progression rates.

claim: About 2% of cells expressing GFP-SOD1wt were positive for anti-NLP staining.
source: We found that about 2% of the cells expressing GFP-SOD1wt were positive for anti-NLP staining, suggesting that the NES-like sequence is exposed in misfolded wt SOD1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Wt-SOD1 can become misfolded under certain stress conditions and adopt a 'toxic conformation' similar to ALS-linked SOD1 mutants.
source: In support for this observation, previous studies have shown that wt-SOD1 can become misfolded under certain stress conditions and the misfolded wt-SOD1 adopts a 'toxic conformation' that is similar to ALS-linked SOD1 mutants (Rotunno and Bosco, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Zinc binding stabilizes wt-SOD1.
source: It was reported that zinc binding stabilizes wt-SOD1, whereas chelation of zinc leads SOD1 to adopt a 'mutant-like conformation' (Homma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Chelation of zinc leads SOD1 to adopt a 'mutant-like conformation'.
source: It was reported that zinc binding stabilizes wt-SOD1, whereas chelation of zinc leads SOD1 to adopt a 'mutant-like conformation' (Homma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TPEN treatment increases the percentage of cells losing nuclear distribution of GFP-SOD1wt and these cells are specifically stained by anti-NLP.
source: More cells lost nuclear distribution of GFP-SOD1wt following TPEN treatment, and these cells were specifically stained by anti-NLP (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Anti-NLP stains endogenous SOD1 in TPEN-treated cells.
source: Anti-NLP also stained endogenous SOD1 in TPEN-treated cells, whereas a non-conformation-specific anti-SOD1 antibody (71G8) stained both control and TPEN-treated cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Misfolded endogenous SOD1 is exported from the nucleus in TPEN-treated cells.
source: Moreover, in TPEN-treated cells, both 71G8 and anti-NLP showed predominantly cytoplasmic staining (Figure 4E), suggesting that misfolded endogenous SOD1 is also exported from the nucleus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of SOD1 expression dramatically decreases staining by both 71G8 and anti-NLP.
source: The specificity of anti-NLP staining of endogenous SOD1 was demonstrated by siRNA-mediated knockdown of SOD1 expression. RNAi dramatically decreased the staining by both 71G8 and anti-NLP staining (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cells treated with sodium arsenite are specifically stained by anti-NLP, and the staining is significantly reduced when SOD1 is knocked down.
source: Similarly, cells treated with sodium arsenite, an oxidative stress inducer, were also specifically stained by anti-NLP, and the staining was significantly reduced when SOD1 was knocked down (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: DTT treatment results in predominantly cytoplasmic staining of anti-NLP in HeLa cells.
source: Treatment of HeLa cells with dithiothreitol (DTT), a strong reducing agent that may break the disulfide bond in SOD1, also resulted in predominantly cytoplasmic staining of anti-NLP (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: LMB treatment of DTT-treated cells increases anti-NLP staining in the nucleus.
source: LMB treatment of DTT-treated cells increased anti-NLP staining in the nucleus (Figure 4F), indicating that the reduced nuclear staining is due to CRM1-dependent nuclear export of misfolded SOD1.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Certain environmental stresses can induce wt-SOD1 to adopt 'mutant-like' conformation with exposed NES-like sequence.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that certain environmental stresses can induce wt-SOD1 to adopt 'mutant-like' conformation with exposed NES-like sequence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing stress-induced exposure of NES-like sequence in wt-SOD1.

claim: Motor neurons and neurites in spinal cord sections from SOD1L126Z transgenic mice are anti-NLP positive.
source: Conversely, the motor neurons and neurites in the spinal cord sections from SOD1L126Z transgenic mice were anti-NLP positive (Figure 5B) (Deng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Anti-NLP staining is predominantly cytoplasmic in most anterior horn neurons in SOD1L126Z transgenic mice.
source: In addition, the staining was predominantly cytoplasmic in most anterior horn neurons, which is consistent with the distribution pattern we have shown in HeLa cells for GFP-SOD1L126Z (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Anti-NLP staining appears cytoplasmic, both diffuse and as aggregates, in anterior horn neurons and neurites in spinal cord sections from ALS patients harboring A4V or G85R mutation.
source: The anti-NLP staining appeared cytoplasmic, both defuse and as aggregates, in anterior horn neurons and neurites (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: L42Q substitution is expected to disrupt the NES consensus sequence without affecting SOD1 structure.
source: As shown earlier in Figures 2E and 3A, Leu42, one of the NES consensus residue in human SOD1, normally exists as Gln (Q) in mouse and is exposed on the SOD1 protein surface. Therefore, a L42Q substitution is expected to disrupt the NES consensus sequence without affecting SOD1 structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and sequence comparison.

claim: GFP-SOD1wt, GFP-SOD1L42Q, and GFP-SOD1G85R/L42Q are localized in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm in NSC34 cells.
source: As expected, GFP-SOD1wt, GFP-SOD1L42Q, and GFP-SOD1G85R/L42Q were localized in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm, whereas GFP-SOD1G85R was primarily in the cytoplasm (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GFP-SOD1G85R is primarily localized in the cytoplasm in NSC34 cells.
source: As expected, GFP-SOD1wt, GFP-SOD1L42Q, and GFP-SOD1G85R/L42Q were localized in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm, whereas GFP-SOD1G85R was primarily in the cytoplasm (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GFP-SOD1L42Q is not recognized by anti-NLP in native IP.
source: Importantly, native IP showed that GFP-SOD1L42Q was not recognized by anti-NLP, whereas about same amounts of GFP-SOD1G85R/L42Q and GFP-SOD1G85R were precipitated (Figure 6B), supporting that L42Q mutation has little or no effects on SOD1 folding.
evidence: This is supported by native immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: About same amounts of GFP-SOD1G85R/L42Q and GFP-SOD1G85R are precipitated by anti-NLP in native IP.
source: Importantly, native IP showed that GFP-SOD1L42Q was not recognized by anti-NLP, whereas about same amounts of GFP-SOD1G85R/L42Q and GFP-SOD1G85R were precipitated (Figure 6B), supporting that L42Q mutation has little or no effects on SOD1 folding.
evidence: This is supported by native immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: L42Q mutation has little or no effects on SOD1 folding.
source: Importantly, native IP showed that GFP-SOD1L42Q was not recognized by anti-NLP, whereas about same amounts of GFP-SOD1G85R/L42Q and GFP-SOD1G85R were precipitated (Figure 6B), supporting that L42Q mutation has little or no effects on SOD1 folding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the native IP data showing that G85R/L42Q is still recognized by anti-NLP.

claim: Viability is similar for NSC34 cells expressing GFP-SOD1wt and GFP-SOD1L42Q.
source: Viability was similar for cells expressing GFP-SOD1wt and GFP-SOD1L42Q but significantly decreased in cells expressing GFP-SOD1G85R (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by WST-1 cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Viability is significantly decreased in NSC34 cells expressing GFP-SOD1G85R compared to cells expressing GFP-SOD1wt.
source: Viability was similar for cells expressing GFP-SOD1wt and GFP-SOD1L42Q but significantly decreased in cells expressing GFP-SOD1G85R (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by WST-1 cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NSC34 cells expressing GFP-SOD1G85R/L42Q show lower viability than those expressing GFP-SOD1G85R.
source: Cells expressing GFP-SOD1G85R/L42Q showed lower viability than those expressing GFP-SOD1G85R, suggesting that disruption of the NES by L42Q mutation increases the cytotoxicity of GFP-SOD1G85R (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by WST-1 cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Disruption of the NES by L42Q mutation increases the cytotoxicity of GFP-SOD1G85R.
source: Cells expressing GFP-SOD1G85R/L42Q showed lower viability than those expressing GFP-SOD1G85R, suggesting that disruption of the NES by L42Q mutation increases the cytotoxicity of GFP-SOD1G85R (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cell viability data.

claim: Nuclear export of SOD1 mutants plays a defensive role against proteotoxicity in the nucleus.
source: These results suggest that nuclear export of SOD1 mutants plays a defensive role against proteotoxicity in the nucleus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cell viability data showing increased toxicity when nuclear export is disrupted.

claim: SOD1wt-YFP and SOD1L42Q-YFP are localized in both the cytoplasm and the nucleus of neurons throughout the lifespan of C. elegans.
source: As observed in cultured cells, SOD1wt-YFP and SOD1L42Q-YFP were localized in both the cytoplasm and the nucleus of the neurons throughout the lifespan of C. elegans (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: SOD1G85R-YFP is cleared from the nuclei of motor neurons in both L1 and adult C. elegans.
source: SOD1G85R-YFP was cleared from the nuclei of motor neurons in both L1 and adult C. elegans (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP is localized in both the cytoplasm and the nuclei in motor neurons in L1 C. elegans.
source: In contrast, SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP was localized in both the cytoplasm and the nuclei in motor neurons in L1 C. elegans (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Nuclear localization of SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP is only observed in a fraction of neurons in adult C. elegans.
source: In adult C. elegans, the nuclear localization of SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP was only observed in a fraction of the neurons and no visible aggregate was observed in the nucleus. (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP forms large cytoplasmic aggregates in adult C. elegans.
source: Indeed, we found that in adult C. elegans, like SOD1G85R-YFP, SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP formed large cytoplasmic aggregates (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Cytoplasmic aggregation of the mutant protein prevents its entry into the nucleus in adult C. elegans.
source: A possible explanation is that cytoplasmic aggregation of the mutant protein prevents its entry into the nucleus.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the observation that nuclear localization is reduced in adult worms.

claim: Similar amounts of SOD1G85R-YFP and SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP, but not SOD1wt-YFP or SOD1L42Q-YFP, are detected in the insoluble fractions in C. elegans.
source: Similar amount of SOD1G85R-YFP and SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP, but not SOD1wt-YFP or SOD1L42Q-YFP were detected in the insoluble fractions (Figure 7C, upper panel, lanes 2, 6–8), indicating the formation of aggregates for the variants in these C. elegans lines.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: C. elegans lines expressing SOD1wt-YFP and SOD1L42Q-YFP show significantly higher bending rates than SOD1G85R-YFP and SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP lines.
source: As controls, the lines expressing SOD1wt-YFP and SOD1L42Q-YFP showed significantly higher bending rates than SOD1G85R-YFP and SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP lines (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by body bending rate data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: All three SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP lines show significantly lower bending rates than the SOD1G85R-YFP line.
source: Importantly, all three SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP lines showed significantly lower bending rates than the SOD1G85R-YFP line (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by body bending rate data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: SOD1L42Q-YFP and SOD1wt-YFP worms show similar survival rates.
source: SOD1L42Q-YFP and SOD1wt-YFP worms showed similar survival rates, whereas the SOD1G85R-YFP line had significantly decreased survival rate, in agreement with previous reports.
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SOD1G85R-YFP line has significantly decreased survival rate compared to SOD1wt-YFP.
source: SOD1L42Q-YFP and SOD1wt-YFP worms showed similar survival rates, whereas the SOD1G85R-YFP line had significantly decreased survival rate, in agreement with previous reports.
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data presented in the manuscript.

claim: About 80% of all worms expressing SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP died by day 3.
source: Remarkably, about 80% of all worms expressing SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP died by day 3 (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: About 70% of SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP worms show the bagging phenotype, with an average of 4.2 eggs hatched per mother.
source: About 70% of SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP worms showed the bagging phenotype, with an average of 4.2 eggs hatched per mother.
evidence: This is supported by bagging phenotype data presented in the manuscript.

claim: About 17% of SOD1G85R-YFP worms show the bagging phenotype, with an average of 2.4 eggs hatched per mother.
source: This was significantly worse than observed for SOD1G85R-YFP animals, where about 17% of worms showed a bagging phenotype, with an average of 2.4 eggs hatched per mother (Figure 9A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by bagging phenotype data shown in Figure 9A, 9B, and 9C.

claim: Less eggs are laid by SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP animals in 48 hr compared to other lines.
source: Remarkably, less eggs were laid by SOD1G85R/L42Q-YFP animals in 48 hr compared to other lines (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by egg-laying data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Results from cell and animal models indicate that accumulation of misfolded SOD1 in both the cytoplasm and nucleus is more toxic than accumulation only in the cytoplasm.
source: Taken together, results from the cell and the animal models indicate that accumulation of misfolded SOD1 in both the cytoplasm and nucleus is more toxic than accumulation only in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined data from cell viability and C. elegans phenotypic assays.

claim: Removal of misfolded SOD1 from the nucleus, mediated by the exposed NES-like sequence and CRM1-dependent nuclear export, is potentially a defense mechanism against the proteotoxic effects of ALS-linked SOD1 mutants in the nucleus.
source: Therefore, removal of the misfolded SOD1 from the nucleus, mediated by the exposed NES-like sequence and CRM1-dependent nuclear export, is potentially a defense mechanism against the proteotoxic effects of ALS-linked SOD1 mutants in the nucleus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined experimental data.

claim: Exposure of the NES-like sequence is a disease-modifying feature for SOD1 mutants.
source: Our data also suggest that the exposure of the NES-like sequence is a disease-modifying feature for SOD1 mutants.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the correlation with disease progression and toxicity data.

claim: The ability of neurons to remove misfolded proteins from the nucleus after exposure of the NES-like sequence may play an important role in pathogenesis of SOD1-linked ALS.
source: Therefore, the ability of neurons to remove misfolded proteins from the nucleus after exposure of the NES-like sequence may play an important role in pathogenesis of SOD1-linked ALS.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Nuclear export not only decreases the levels of SOD1 mutants in the nucleus, but also increases their levels in the cytoplasm.
source: Nuclear export not only decreases the levels of SOD1 mutants in the nucleus, but also increases their levels in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the mechanism of nuclear export.

claim: Loss of nuclear SOD1 is unlikely a disease mechanism because SOD1 knockout does not lead to ALS phenotype and pathology.
source: Loss of nuclear SOD1 may lead to loss of function in the nucleus, but it is unlikely a disease mechanism because SOD1 knockout does not lead to ALS phenotype and pathology (Reaume et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an inference based on citation to previous literature showing SOD1 knockout mice do not develop ALS.

claim: Knockdown of SOD1 mutants by siRNA is currently being pursued as a therapeutic approach for ALS.
source: To the contrary, knockdown of SOD1 mutants by siRNA are currently being pursued as a therapeutic approach for ALS (Ralph et al., 2005; Thomsen et al., 2014; van Zundert and Brown, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Nuclear export may facilitate the removal of misfolded SOD1, which would produce beneficial effects.
source: Nuclear export may facilitate the removal of misfolded SOD1, which would produce beneficial effects.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential beneficial effects of nuclear export.

claim: The nucleus relies exclusively on the proteasomal degradation pathway to remove misfolded and unwanted proteins.
source: It is known that the nucleus relies on exclusively the proteasomal degradation pathway to remove misfolded and unwanted proteins, whereas the cytoplasm has both proteasomal and lysosome-dependent autophagy pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular protein degradation pathways.

claim: The cytoplasm has both proteasomal and lysosome-dependent autophagy pathways for protein degradation.
source: It is known that the nucleus relies on exclusively the proteasomal degradation pathway to remove misfolded and unwanted proteins, whereas the cytoplasm has both proteasomal and lysosome-dependent autophagy pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular protein degradation pathways.

claim: Nuclear export may facilitate mutant SOD1 degradation by autophagy.
source: Thus, nuclear export may facilitate mutant SOD1 degradation by autophagy.
evidence: This is speculation based on the availability of autophagy in the cytoplasm.

claim: Nuclear export increases the cytoplasmic concentration of abnormal SOD1, which may promote toxic effects on the functions of cytoplasmic organelles.
source: On the other hand, nuclear export increases the cytoplasmic concentration of the abnormal SOD1, which may promote toxic effects on the functions of cytoplasmic organelles, for example, ER and mitochondria.
evidence: This is speculation about potential negative effects of nuclear export.

claim: NES-like sequence-mediated changes in subcellular localization of SOD1 mutants may have complex effects on neuronal functions and survival, but collectively, may reduce the toxicity of SOD1 mutants.
source: It is likely that NES-like sequence-mediated changes in subcellular localization of SOD1 mutants would have complex effects on neuronal functions and survival, but collectively, may reduce the toxicity of SOD1 mutants.
evidence: This is speculation and interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: Exposure of the NES-like sequence may be a common property of misfolded SOD1.
source: Our results also indicate that exposure of the NES-like sequence may be a common property of misfolded SOD1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing NES exposure in multiple mutants and misfolded wt-SOD1.

claim: Misfolding of wt-SOD1 is involved in pathogenesis of sporadic ALS.
source: Misfolded wt-SOD1 also shares this feature, which supports the controversial proposition that misfolding of wt-SOD1 is involved in pathogenesis of sporadic ALS (Rotunno and Bosco, 2013; van Zundert and Brown, 2017; Ayers et al., 2016; Grad et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and the experimental data showing NES exposure in misfolded wt-SOD1.

claim: The exposure of NES-like sequence can be specifically detected with anti-NLP antibody.
source: The exposure of NES-like sequence can be specifically detected with anti-NLP antibody, which may become a useful tool for research and diagnosis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the antibody specificity data and speculation about its utility.

claim: Several antibodies that recognize regions covered or partially overlapping with the NES-like sequence have been reported, including D3H5, AJ10, and USOD.
source: Interestingly, several other antibodies that recognize regions covered or partially overlapping with the NES-like sequence have been reported, including D3H5 (epitope: residues 24–55) (Rotunno and Bosco, 2013; Gros-Louis et al., 2010), AJ10 (epitope: residues 29–57) (Sábado et al., 2013), and USOD (epitope: residues 42–48) (Kerman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Antibodies D3H5, AJ10, and USOD selectively recognize mutant SOD1 over wt-SOD1.
source: All these antibodies were also reported to selectively recognize mutant SOD1 over wt-SOD1, suggesting that the epitopes formed by the NES-like sequence are highly specific for misfolded SOD1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The epitopes formed by the NES-like sequence are highly specific for misfolded SOD1.
source: All these antibodies were also reported to selectively recognize mutant SOD1 over wt-SOD1, suggesting that the epitopes formed by the NES-like sequence are highly specific for misfolded SOD1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective recognition by multiple antibodies.

claim: The NES-like sequence may serve as a biomarker for the detection of misfolded SOD1 in ALS patients.
source: Therefore, the NES-like sequence may serve as a biomarker for the detection of misfolded SOD1 in ALS patients.
evidence: This is speculation based on the specificity of the NES-like sequence for misfolded SOD1.

claim: The immunogenic region may be used for immunotherapy for SOD1-linked ALS.
source: Moreover, this immunogenic region may be used for immunotherapy for SOD1-linked ALS as was reported for the SOD1 exposed dimer interface (SEDI) peptide, that is specifically exposed in monomeric SOD1 (Rakhit et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to previous immunotherapy approaches.

claim: Proper maintenance of nuclear protein homeostasis is important for preserving cell function.
source: Proper maintenance of nuclear protein homeostasis is important for preserving cell function (Shibata and Morimoto, 2014; Gallagher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in the nucleus can affect cell function and cause diseases.
source: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in the nucleus can affect cell function and cause diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: A number of neurodegenerative diseases are associated with aggregates and inclusions formed by misfolded proteins in the nucleus.
source: A number of neurodegenerative diseases are associated with aggregates and inclusions formed by misfolded proteins in the nucleus, such as polyglutamine (polyQ) repeat diseases, polyalanine (polyA) repeat diseases, the RNA-mediated diseases, neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease (NIID), neuronal intermediate filament inclusion disease (NIFID), multiple system atrophy (MSA), neuroferritinopathy, and inclusion body myopathy with early onset Paget's disease and frontotemporal dementia (IBMPFD) (Gallagher et al., 2014; Woulfe, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Exposure of a normally buried NES-like sequence leading to CRM1-dependent nuclear export of misfolded SOD1 may represent a novel mechanism for maintaining nuclear proteostasis.
source: In addition to the known protein quality control mechanisms, such as chaperones and ubiquitin-proteasome system (Shibata and Morimoto, 2014; Gallagher et al., 2014), our findings suggest that exposure of a normally buried NES-like sequence leading to CRM1-dependent nuclear export of the misfolded SOD1 may represent a novel mechanism for maintaining nuclear proteostasis.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Exposure of normally buried hydrophobic regions is a common feature of misfolded proteins.
source: Exposure of normally buried hydrophobic regions is a common feature of misfolded proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein misfolding.

claim: Hydrophobic regions are commonly recognized by chaperones and quality control E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: These hydrophobic regions are commonly recognized by chaperones and quality control E3 ubiquitin ligases, to initiate the refolding and ubiquitination of the misfolded proteins, respectively (Rosenbaum et al., 2011; Fredrickson et al., 2013; Horwich, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: NES consensus sequences are frequently observed in hydrophobic regions buried inside of proteins.
source: Interestingly, proteomic analysis has revealed that NES consensus sequences are frequently observed in hydrophobic regions buried inside of proteins (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Many misfolded proteins may expose buried hydrophobic regions containing NES consensus sequences, which may result in being exported from the nucleus by CRM1.
source: This suggests that many misfolded proteins may expose buried hydrophobic regions containing NES consensus sequences, which may result in being exported from the nucleus by CRM1 if not efficiently degraded by the nuclear proteasomes or refolded by chaperones.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and the prevalence of buried NES sequences.

claim: Nuclear export may be a mechanism responsible for cytosolic mislocalization of many disease-causing mutant proteins.
source: Nuclear export may be a mechanism responsible for cytosolic mislocalization of many disease-causing mutant proteins (Hung and Link, 2011).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mutations in the NLS of FUS lead to its mislocalization to the cytoplasm.
source: For example, mutations in the NLS of FUS, which also cause ALS, leads to its mislocalization to the cytoplasm (Dormann et al., 2010; Gal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mutations in TDP43 lead to exclusion of TDP43 protein from the nucleus of neurons and the formation of cytoplasmic TDP43 aggregates.
source: Mutations in another ALS-linked gene, TDP43, also lead to exclusion of TDP43 protein from the nucleus of the neurons and the formation of cytoplasmic TDP43 aggregates, but the underlying mechanism is not clear (Mackenzie et al., 2007; Deng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Abnormal nucleocytoplasmic transport may represent a convergent pathogenic pathway for some neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Abnormal nucleocytoplasmic transport may represent a convergent pathogenic pathway for some neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observations of mislocalization in multiple disease proteins.

claim: Nuclear-cytoplasmic transport is disrupted by the hexanucleotide repeat expansion (HRE) GGGGCC (G4C2) in C9orf72, which causes ALS and frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
source: Most recent studies have suggested that the nuclear-cytoplasmic transport is disrupted by the hexanucleotide repeat expansion (HRE) GGGGCC (G4C2) in C9orf72, which causes ALS and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (Zhang et al., 2015; Freibaum et al., 2015; Jovičić et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The exposure of NES-like sequence in mutant and misfolded SOD1 may affect the nucleocytoplasmic transport of other cargo.
source: It is possible that the exposure of NES-like sequence in mutant and misfolded SOD1 may also affect the nucleocytoplasmic transport of other cargo, because CRM1-mediated export is saturable and SOD1 is a highly abundant protein in the cell.
evidence: This is speculation based on the abundance of SOD1 and the saturable nature of CRM1-mediated export.

claim: Nuclear export is deleterious in C9orf72-caused ALS, but it is protective in SOD1-linked ALS.
source: However, there is an important distinction that nuclear export is deleterious in C9orf72-caused ALS, but it is protective in SOD1-linked ALS.
evidence: This is an interpretation contrasting the roles of nuclear export in different forms of ALS.
